title: How Antibacterial Soap Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chris Pallette discuss whether antibacterial soap should be outlawed or reconsidered. They argue it is not much more effective than regular soap and may breed stronger, drug-resistant bacteria, citing MRSA (called "Mercia" in the transcript) as an example. They describe the "antibacterial lifestyle" of overusing antibacterial products, the hygiene hypothesis concern that children need some exposure to dirt and germs to build immunity, and alternatives such as bleach, which kills microbes by lysing their cell walls (the origin of the Lysol name, meaning to lyse cells). They also mention a countertop material in development with microscopic surface points that rupture bacteria mechanically. The episode closes with a promo for the article "Should Antibacterial Soap Be Outlawed?" on HowStuffWorks.com. Note: this is a short segment, and the transcript contains speech-recognition errors in names and terms.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic of antibacterial soap and asks whether it should be outlawed; Chris says it should be reconsidered for everyday use.

segments.title: Why antibacterial soap may breed resistant bacteria
segments.summary: The hosts say antibacterial soap is not much more effective than regular soap and can help bacteria that survive evolve resistance. They cite MRSA, a drug-resistant staph, as a dangerous example.

segments.title: The antibacterial lifestyle and childhood exposure to germs
segments.summary: Chris describes the 'antibacterial lifestyle' of products in homes and stores. The hosts argue that over-sanitized environments may prevent children from building immunity and allergy tolerance.

segments.title: Bleach and antimicrobial countertops
segments.summary: They discuss bleach as an alternative that kills microbes by breaching their cell walls, and the Lysol name's origin in cell lysis. They also describe a countertop material in development whose microscopic surface points rupture bacteria without chemicals.

segments.title: Closing and article promotion
segments.summary: Chris says he has given up antibacterial soap, and the hosts promote the HowStuffWorks article on the topic and invite listener feedback.
